hints.title: Express an AP median
hints.body: For an arithmetic progression with first term a and difference d, the median of the first r terms is a+(r−1)d2. This holds for either parity of r and for increasing or decreasing progressions.
hints.recap: The median equals the average of the block endpoints.
hints.pitfall: An even-length median need not itself be a term.

recall.reminder: An odd-length median is a middle entry; an even-length median averages the two middle entries.

hints.title: Compare the median formulae
hints.body: Subtract the first-n median formula from the first-(n+2) formula. To test doubling, try a simple AP with odd difference and odd n.
hints.recap: Parity can affect an even-block median.
hints.pitfall: An example disproves a universal claim only when it satisfies the given median premise.
hints.pause: Decide which conclusion follows from the difference and test the doubling claim.

recall.reminder: Parity can affect an even-block median.

hints.title: Use the selected endpoints
hints.body: Write the first and last terms of the even-index subsequence in terms of the original first term and difference, then average them.
hints.recap: The selected terms themselves form an AP.
hints.pitfall: There are n selected terms, not twice that many.
hints.pause: Simplify its median, test integrality and combine all classifications.

recall.reminder: The selected terms themselves form an AP.

solution:
Let the progression be xr=a+(r−1)d, with integers a and d. The median of its first r terms is Mr=a+(r−1)d2, since the middle term or two middle terms average to the endpoint average.

I: Mn+2=Mn+d, so an integer Mn implies an integer Mn+2. This is true.

II: take xr=r and n=1. The first median is 1 but the median of 1,2 is 32. Thus II is false.

III: the selected AP has endpoints a+d and a+(2n−1)d, so its median is their average a+nd, an integer. This is true.

Answer F: I and III only.
